name: Victor Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm lead operator on the corrugator at a cardboard box plant. The corrugator is the big machine, about a hundred metres long, that glues the wavy paper between two flat sheets to make board, with steam rolls and glue pans and a knife at the end. I start at six, check the glue, check the paper reels, and then mostly listen and watch for warp. When the board comes out curled like a crisp, that's my morning gone.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what gets to you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's physical and you can see what you made, stacks of board taller than me by lunchtime. I like my crew, Bruno and the two Kowalski brothers, we've been together six years. What gets to me is the noise, even with ear defenders, and the paperwork they keep adding. I don't do apps or any of that AI stuff, I've got a phone for calls and the football scores.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, see, nothing to get worked up about. I don't post online, but at the canteen I'd say it to whoever brought it up. Bruno reads all that tech news and I'd enjoy reminding him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means nothing changes, and that suits me. I've got a good job, good pay, and a flat my grandmother left me that I rent out to a young couple. I'm not chasing anything, I just want things to stay sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. I'd keep saving like I do, I put the rent from the flat straight into savings and live off my wages. Maybe Ines and I would finally book a proper holiday, since there's nothing to worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a normal Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything at your plant that AI would touch even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office, maybe, the people who do orders and scheduling. They'd get some program to plan the runs better. As long as the program doesn't tell me how much glue to put on, I don't care what it does upstairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned you don't use apps. Does that ever cause problems at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sometimes. They brought in a tablet for logging downtime and I write it on the sheet and Bruno types it in for me. It works, so why change it. I'll learn it if they make me, but nobody's made me yet.

S0.say: I'd tell whoever brought it up at the canteen that there was nothing to get worked up about. I'd especially enjoy reminding Bruno, who reads all the tech news.
S0.think: For me it means nothing changes, and that suits me fine. I have a good job, good pay and my grandmother's flat rented out, and I just want things to stay sensible.
S0.do: Carries on as now, putting the flat's rent straight into savings and living on wages. Possibly books a proper holiday with Ines since there is nothing to worry about.
S0.quote: As long as the program doesn't tell me how much glue to put on, I don't care what it does upstairs.
S0.fieldNote: Victor wants a quiet, sensible life and has the means for it. He avoids digital tools and gets round them through a colleague rather than learning. His comfort rests on a mix of a good wage and an inherited asset that most operators his age lack.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it makes sense to use machines where they help, but don't go mad with it. I'm not against progress, I'm against change for the sake of a manager's bonus. If someone asked me, I'd say both the companies and the government need to be sensible about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think the corrugator is one of the last machines they'd automate fully, because it's so finicky with paper moisture and weather. But the bits around it, the stacking and the forklift work, those are already going robotic at the big plant across the motorway. So my crew might shrink even if my job stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and see what they actually bring in, I'm not going to panic about something that hasn't happened. If they said I had to learn the new screens, I'd do it, slowly, with someone showing me. I'd keep the flat money going into savings and not take on any new loans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like hearing a funny noise in the car and deciding to wait and see if it gets worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your crew might shrink, you said. How would that be for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bad, honestly. The Kowalski brothers do the stacking end, and that's the first bit to go. Six years I've stood next to those two, and a robot arm could do Piotr's job by Christmas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do anything to protect them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell management they're good workers and should be moved, not let go. But I'm not a union man, I'd do it by talking. And if there are plenty of other plants around, they'd find something, they're hard workers.

S1.say: I'd say use machines where they help but don't go mad with it. I'm not against progress, only change for a manager's bonus, and both companies and government should be sensible.
S1.think: Privately I think the corrugator itself is finicky enough to be automated last, but the stacking and forklift work around it is already going robotic elsewhere. My crew could shrink even if my job stays.
S1.do: Keeps working and waits to see what the plant actually brings in, learning new screens slowly if required. Keeps the flat's rent going into savings and takes on no new loans.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a funny noise in the car he decides to wait on.
S1.quote: Six years I've stood next to those two, and a robot arm could do Piotr's job by Christmas.
S1.fieldNote: Victor's instinct is to wait until a change is real. He feels most for his crew, especially the Kowalski brothers on the stacking end. He prefers to speak up by talking to managers rather than through a union, which fits his middle-ground, non-political stance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't believe it until I see it. But if I did see it, I'd say somebody in charge should have seen this coming and done something. I'm not one for marches, but I'd want answers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it would scare me more than I'd let on. I've only ever done this. I'm good at it, but I picked a job where I'd never have to learn computers, and now the computer is the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything big, no holiday, no new car. I'd keep the flat rented because that money would matter more than ever, and I'd think about Ines and me moving into it ourselves if my wage went, so we'd save our rent. I'd stay at the plant as long as they'd have me, and keep everything in cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach turns just thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd notice at the plant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the engineers from the robot company walking round with clipboards and measuring tape, like they did before the palletiser went in. Everyone goes quiet when that happens. I'd be standing at my machine, pretending not to watch them measure the space where I stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If your job went, what would a normal day look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, and that's what gets me. I'd probably fix up the flat, paint it, do the bathroom. After that, I really don't know, I'm not someone who sits around.

S2.say: I'd say I won't believe it until I see it, but if I did, someone in charge should have seen it coming. I'm not one for marches, but I'd want answers.
S2.think: Privately it would scare me more than I'd show, because I chose a job where I'd never need computers. Now the computer would be the job.
S2.do: Stops all big spending and keeps savings in cash. Keeps the flat rented for the income, considers moving into it with Ines if his wage stops, and stays at the plant as long as possible.
S2.feel: Alarmed, with his stomach turning at the thought.
S2.quote: I'd be standing at my machine, pretending not to watch them measure the space where I stand.
S2.fieldNote: His resistance to technology was a deliberate choice that feels like a trap in this picture. The inherited flat becomes his anchor, both as income and a fallback home. He blames no one in particular but wants those in charge to answer for not seeing it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for the government and the companies to put a plan together, so they'd better. At work I'd tell the lads to save their money and not buy new cars on finance. I wouldn't make a big speech about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think five years is enough to get my house in order but not enough to become a different person. I'd be 32, and I've got no interest in sitting in a classroom. But I'd have to do something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do up the flat properly, new kitchen and bathroom, so it rents for more and keeps its value, maybe ten thousand from savings. I'd keep working and saving and stay at the plant to the end. If there was a practical course, something like maintenance on the new machines that the company paid for, I'd probably do it, but I wouldn't go looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's there in the background most days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't go looking. What if nobody offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd stay put until they showed me the door. I know that's not clever. I'd rather spend five years doing what I'm good at than four years being bad at something new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ines works in a dentist's. What does she think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She thinks dentists will keep people a while longer, because people don't want a robot in their mouth. She'd probably tell me to stop being stubborn and do a course. She's usually right, which is annoying.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for government and companies to make a plan, so they'd better. At work I'd quietly tell the lads to save and avoid car finance.
S3.think: Privately five years is enough to get my house in order but not to become a different person. I'd be 32 with no interest in a classroom, but I'd have to do something.
S3.do: Spends about ten thousand from savings renovating the flat so it rents for more and holds its value. Keeps working and saving at the plant and would take a company-paid maintenance course if offered, without seeking one.
S3.feel: Anxious, with the worry sitting in the background most days.
S3.quote: I'd rather spend five years doing what I'm good at than four years being bad at something new.
S3.fieldNote: Victor puts his effort into the asset he understands, the flat, rather than into himself. He is frank that staying put is not clever but prefers being good at something to being bad at something new. Ines acts as the voice pushing him towards retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, a lot can happen, let's see. I wouldn't want people losing their heads over something that far off. If anything, I'd say the government should start planning now, quietly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think I've got time, which is exactly the thinking that gets people in trouble. I'd be 37 when it arrives, still young enough to do something else, I suppose. I'd mostly put it out of my mind for a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First few years, nothing different, keep working and saving the flat rent. Maybe I'd buy a second small flat with Ines once we'd saved the deposit, because property feels safer to me than anything on a screen. If by year five or six it was clearly happening, I'd look at a course then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but far off. Like knowing you'll need a new roof one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy a second flat. Would people still be able to pay rent if robots do the work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's a good point and I hadn't thought of it. I suppose if nobody has wages, nobody pays rent. I trust bricks more than computers, but bricks still need someone with a wage to live in them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So does that change your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd keep more in savings and buy smaller. I'd still want something real I can stand in. Ask me again in five years.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long time and a lot can happen, so let's see. People shouldn't lose their heads, though the government should start planning quietly now.
S4.think: Privately I'd think I have time, which I know is the thinking that gets people in trouble. I'd be 37, still young enough to change, and I'd put it out of my mind for a while.
S4.do: Keeps working and saving the flat's rent for the first few years. Considers buying a second, smaller flat with Ines and would look at a course around year five or six if it was clearly happening.
S4.feel: Uneasy but distant, like knowing he'll need a new roof one day.
S4.quote: I trust bricks more than computers, but bricks still need someone with a wage to live in them.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Victor push the problem down the road, and he admits that is risky. When asked whether tenants could still pay rent, he stopped and reconsidered his faith in property out loud. His trust in things he can touch runs through every scenario.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have no time to do anything except panic quietly. I picked this job so I'd never have to learn computers, and that one turns my whole plan upside down. What would help is someone giving operators like me a practical, paid course, at the plant, with a real job at the end, not a website.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what we do with all the free time. People like me don't do well sitting around. If there's no work, there'd better be something to do with your hands.

headlineQuote: I picked this job so I'd never have to learn computers, and that one turns my whole plan upside down.
portrait: Victor Ziegler, 27, is lead operator on a corrugator at a cardboard box plant. He is practical, unpolitical and proudly offline, and his safety net is a flat his grandmother left him, which he rents out. A plateau suits him perfectly and steady disruption mostly worries him for his crew on the stacking end. Fast AGI alarms him, because he chose a job where he would never need computers, and he falls back on the flat as income and possible home. With five or ten years he puts his effort into property rather than retraining, while admitting this is stubborn and questioning his own plan out loud.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there would be no time to do anything except panic quietly.
whatWouldHelp: A practical, paid course at the plant for operators like him, with a real job at the end rather than a website.
